newsitem.title: USA: People get passionate about personal Web pages.
newsitem.headline: People get passionate about personal Web pages.

text.p: People do amazing things in their spare time.
Take Dan Hildreth. The 24-year-old Waukee, Iowa, resident spends a dozen hours or more a week updating his personal home page, The Viking Underground (http://www.dwx.com/(tilde)vikings/).

An homage to the Minnesota Vikings pro football team, Hildreth's Web site includes everything a fan could want, including game scores and stats during the season, and during the off season, information on trades, training camp and the annual Viking fan convention.

Derek M. Powazek, a 23-year-old San Francisco man, spends evenings and weekends tinkering with his home page, The Fray (http://www.fray.com/), an online celebration of storytelling and art where people write about the most tender, shocking or revealing moments of their lives and readers follow up with their own experiences and views.

Though completely different, The Viking Underground and The Fray show how far personal home pages have come since people first discovered the Web could serve as an inexpensive, simple-to-learn publishing medium.
NetGuide magazine recently honoured Hildreth, Powazek and six other Web auteurs -- some amateurs, some professionals -- for their inventive, informative, and sometimes humorous personal Web pages.

Other sites the magazine recognised for their individuality and flair included Grrl Enterprises (http://www.grrl.com), girl-talk about friends, dating, diets and work; Crazy World, (http://open.hr/tvazdar), the life and times of Croat Tomislav Vazdar; and The Labyrinth (http://www.labryinth.com/), a Los Angeles multimedia artist's private showcase.

Creating a home page has never been simpler. All you really need is an idea, some time and a few simple tools. The past two years has seen a proliferation of software for converting plain text to HTML, the programming code Web pages are written in, as well as programmes such as Adobe Photoshop for creating Web graphics.
Internet service providers encourage customers' home-page publishing urges by including a few megabytes of space on the companies' Web servers in the price of a low-cost dial-up account.

Online networks such as America Online (http://www.aol.com/) and Prodigy (http://www.prodigy.com/) and Web sites such as Tripod (http://www.tripod.com/) and GeoCities (http://www.geocities.com/) make it even easier, giving subscribers a standardised Web-page form called a template. Fill in the blanks, and presto, you're a Webmaster.
But, according to the NetGuide honourees, there's more to publishing a really good personal Web page than the mechanics.
"Make sure it's not just copying other people's work or you'll get flamed big time," advises Bonnie Burton, creator of Grrl Enterprises, and an editor for AtHome Network (http://www.athome.net/).
Other advice:

-- Love what you're doing, or you'll quickly lose interest. "If you want something to be cool, something you can be proud of, you'll spend a lot of time on it" and if you don't care about it to begin with you'll quickly get bored, Burton said.
-- Research what's already out there, and make what you do different.

-- Experiment. Multimedia artist Amy Seidman's personal page, The Labyrinth, is an online maze full of interactive stories, video clips, music and poetry the ex-photographer put together a year ago to teach herself about Web design. "I wanted a place where I could experiment with ideas before I pitched them to clients and have an online portfolio," Seidman said.
-- Commit to regular updates. Most of the home-page creators NetGuide honoured update their Web sites every day, or at least every week.

-- Provide information, even if it's on an obscure topic. Vazdar, who lives in Zagreb, includes extensive information about Croatia in his home page. "Very often I have to answer questions about the political and economic situation in this region," he said.
-- Don't get sucked into design fads such as blinking text or rainbow-coloured buttons and lines.

By their definition, a personal Web pages is a labour of love, not a money-making proposition. Powazek, who earns a living as a section producer at the Electronic Minds (http://www.minds.com/) Web site, would love it if The Fray could support him, but that would mean accepting advertising, something he'd never do.
"It just wouldn't jive," he said.

Working on a personal home page can have unexpected positive results. With what he taught himself working on The Viking Underground for two years, Hildreth was able to dump his old career as a credit counsellor for a job as a technical-support representative for a Des Moines, Iowa, Internet service provider.
"People say if you put your mind to it you can do anything you want to. That came true for me," he said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
